messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was fifty-two when the hurricane tore through the coastal district. He stood on the metal grating of the municipal archive roof, wrestling with heavy tarp straps, when the wind shifted without warning. One moment the storm was a steady, heavy roar; the next, a steel support beam gave way with a sharp, explosive crack that echoed like a detonation. People on the ground began shouting, their voices rising in overlapping panic, and the sudden gusts whipped debris against the scaffolding. The storm passed over the course of hours, but it was the unpredictability of those shifting winds, the sharp cracks, and the rising shouts that settled into his routine. In the weeks that followed, Kwame found his body bracing before his mind caught up. A backfiring car would make his shoulders hike to his ears; a dropped metal tray in the breakroom sent a jolt through his ribs. He would catch himself breathing hard, certain the storm was returning, even though the sky was clear. His wife, Nia, noticed how he started leaving the house earlier to avoid rush hour, skipping gatherings where conversations grew too loud or plans shifted too quickly. He kept his mind occupied—tuning radios, solving crosswords in the paper, watching construction videos on his tablet—and sitting still made the quiet feel heavy. When he finally let himself remember the night on the roof, the fragments would not hold together. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, letting the details slip back into the quiet. The picture remained incomplete, parts of the night drifting just out of reach. On more than one occasion, the weight of the tarp straps would return in a wave, and for a few seconds he was standing on the roof again, the wind biting his neck. When the pieces did surface, a hot surge of rage would rise in his chest, fierce and sudden. His work at the county bomb disposal unit became a familiar ground, yet also a place where his reactions played out in plain sight. During a live training exercise, a sudden hydraulic hiss from a cutting torch made him step back, his body already coiled, before the technician even called out. The unpredictability of the unit’s dispatch schedule mirrored the way the storm had arrived. He learned to navigate the workshop with a quiet rhythm, deliberately taking the stairs instead of the elevator to avoid the sudden jolt of the doors, carrying snacks he ate methodically to manage the rising tension. When his supervisor scheduled an unexpected site visit, Kwame felt the familiar tightness in his throat and quietly declined, preferring the controlled clutter of his workbench to the shifting demands of the office. His recent intake screening yielded a PCL-5 score of sixty-four, a number that felt accurate to the weight he had been carrying. Now at fifty-five, Kwame sits across from me with his hands folded, the calluses from wire cutters still visible. He came in because the quiet at home no longer feels safe. He worries that if he stops moving or stops eating, the tension will build until he snaps. What he hopes for is not the complete erasure of the memories, but the space to remember them without the room tilting beneath him. He is learning that the body’s early warning is not a signal of catastrophe, and that the shouting of a crowd or the crack of a door is not a return of the storm, but simply the world moving forward.
